ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Otolaryngology Consultation — Amelia Earhart

code.originalText: Nasal endoscopy and otolaryngology consultation: diagnosis, an acute exacerbation, and the plan for imaging and surgery

text.paragraph: Suspected chronic rhinosinusitis in a 25-year-old private pilot with five months of nasal blockage, discolored drainage, left cheek and forehead pressure, reduced smell, and pressure pain on descent when flying. Anterior rhinoscopy showed swollen turbinates without visible polyps or pus. She started saline irrigation and fluticasone today. Please confirm the diagnosis by nasal endoscopy, say whether polyps are present, and advise on further treatment, imaging, surgery, and flying. [S]

list.item: Does she have chronic rhinosinusitis, and are nasal polyps present?
Is saline irrigation with an intranasal steroid the right first treatment, and is there a place for an antibiotic or an oral steroid?
When should a sinus CT be done, and when would endoscopic sinus surgery help her?
Is there anything that changes management, such as allergy, immune deficiency, a dental source, or her past sinus operations?
When can she fly, which medicines can she use as a pilot, and how can she avoid sinus and ear barotrauma?

text.paragraph: Ms. Earhart, a 25-year-old private pilot, is seen at the request of Dr. Talbot. She has had five months of nasal blockage, discolored drainage, pressure over the left cheek and forehead, and reduced smell, with pressure pain on descent when flying. Years ago a severe sinus infection during an influenza illness was treated in hospital with drainage operations; she does not know which sinuses were opened. She started saline irrigation and fluticasone two weeks ago. Five days ago the left side worsened, with thicker yellow-green drainage, more pressure, and aching left upper teeth. She has no asthma, aspirin sensitivity, or frequent infections, and has never smoked. She has not flown since the first visit. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Amelia Mary Earhart was born on July 24, 1897, in Atchison, Kansas, to Amy Otis and Edwin Stanton Earhart. [D]

After visiting her sister in Toronto at Christmas 1917, she moved there in February 1918 and worked in the Voluntary Aid Detachment at the Spadina Military Hospital, often on twelve-hour shifts, going wherever an extra pair of hands was needed. [D]

During the 1918 influenza epidemic she worked nights on the ward that held the influenza patients; within weeks she fell ill herself, with severe sinus pain and terrible headaches. Her case was serious enough that doctors operated, opening into her sinuses so that they could be drained regularly. It was a month before she was well enough to leave hospital, and she went to recover at her sister's home in Massachusetts. [D]
She suffered from chronic sinus problems for the rest of her life. [D]

She entered Columbia University as a pre-medical student in the fall of 1919 and left in 1920. She took her first airplane ride in December 1920, with the pilot Frank Hawks, and became a licensed pilot in the early 1920s: Purdue University dates her pilot's license to May 1923, and the Encyclopedia of the Great Plains to 1921. [D]

In modern terms, sinus disease that began with a severe sinus infection during influenza, needed drainage operations, and caused lasting headaches and sinus trouble fits chronic rhinosinusitis. The fetched sources give no diagnosis in those terms, and nothing is known of her sinus anatomy or of nasal polyps. [R]

list.item: Chronic rhinosinusitis without nasal polyps (J32.9). Her symptoms for more than 12 weeks with edema and pus in the middle meatus on endoscopy confirm chronic rhinosinusitis, as the AAO-HNS guideline requires; there are no polyps, and normal eosinophils and IgE without asthma suggest disease without type 2 inflammation. The worsening of the past five days is an acute exacerbation with pus, and a short course of amoxicillin-clavulanate, guided by the culture, is reasonable. An oral steroid is not advised, because the evidence for it is in disease with polyps. Saline irrigation and an intranasal steroid remain the basis of treatment. A CT is not needed now: there are no warning signs, and a CT is best done after about eight more weeks of medical therapy if symptoms persist, to judge whether surgery is appropriate and to plan it. Surgery is appropriate if the CT shows disease and the SNOT-22 stays at 20 or more after that therapy; it is her choice. The aching left upper teeth deserve a dental check, because a dental source can cause one-sided disease. Her old drainage operations do not change this plan; the CT will show any scarring. For flying: she must not fly while blocked or in pain, because a blocked sinus or ear cannot equalize on descent; the saline rinse and nasal steroid are acceptable for pilots; any new medicine needs a 48-hour ground trial; sedating antihistamines are no-go medicines. A decongestant does not make it safe to fly with a cold. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Talbot's intake note. Eosinophils 0.21 x10^3/uL and total IgE 42 IU/mL, both normal. SNOT-22 52 at intake and 58 today; facial pain 6 of 10 at intake and 7 today. No imaging. [S]

list.item: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily with food for 10 days for the acute exacerbation; adjust to the culture result. [S]
No oral corticosteroid and no antifungal treatment. [S]
Continue high-volume saline irrigation twice daily and fluticasone two sprays in each nostril daily. [S]
SNOT-22 during treatment and at about ten weeks; CT of the sinuses without contrast before the ten-week review if symptoms persist. [S]
Offer endoscopic sinus surgery if the CT shows disease and the SNOT-22 is 20 or more after appropriate medical therapy, as a shared decision. [S]
Dental check for the aching left upper teeth. [S]
No flying while blocked or in pain; a 48-hour ground trial of each new medicine; no sedating antihistamines; clear the ears and sinuses early and often on descent. [S]
Seek care at once for eye swelling, vision change, severe headache, stiff neck, or confusion. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Talbot, who sees her the same day. The endoscopy findings were shown and explained to Ms. Earhart, who agreed to the antibiotic course and the plan for a CT only if needed; she decides who else receives this note. [S]
Follow-up: Otolaryngology review of the CT and the SNOT-22 at about ten weeks, or sooner for warning signs; Dr. Talbot continues primary management. [S]
